description: NASA embarked on a journey beyond Earth. Where is Earth? This is what the "X Voyagers" asked themselves. To find the answer, NASA created the "X Voyagers" mission, a mission that did not seek answers (for the mission itself *was* an answer)
summary:
What should we do with the machines we leave behind in space?

The X Voyager is a 3D browser game where school-age learners investigate NASA equipment on the Moon and Mars. From a fictional museum in Yucatán, players choose one of ten expeditions and visit equipment such as Surveyor 3 and Viking 1. They collect observations and photos in a field journal and use NASA mission records to learn what each machine helped scientists discover.

Then they decide whether to bring the equipment back to the museum or preserve it at its site. They explain their choice using what they found. Two students can explore the same mission, reach different conclusions and discuss the evidence behind their decisions.
details:
What players do

The X Voyager turns NASA’s discarded-equipment storytelling challenge into a playable expedition. Players start in a fictional museum in Yucatán, where two holograms open the Moon and Mars briefings. Diana guides the lunar expeditions, and Tudor guides the Mars expeditions.

At each site, players examine the equipment, record an observation, and take three photos. They read a short mission briefing and answer a question before deciding whether to recover the equipment or preserve it where it stands. They write a reason in their journal and return to the museum. A recovered object appears in its exhibit.

How we used NASA resources

NASA mission records informed the historical briefings and questions. On the Moon, players learn what Surveyor 3’s camera and scoop helped scientists study. On Mars, Viking 1 introduces them to the study of Martian soil, weather, and possible signs of life.

NASA archival images and reference materials inform the exhibits. The project also uses NASA planet imagery and an Extravehicular Mobility Unit model. Each historical source is credited in the game. The museum, guides, and recovery decisions are part of the fictional story.

Why we built it

We designed the game so students can explain why a mission mattered and use evidence to defend a choice. In a classroom, two students can investigate the same site and discuss why one would bring the equipment home while the other would preserve it in place.

How we built and tested it

The game uses Next.js, React, TypeScript, Three.js, and WebGL. Players can start as guests. Supabase supports optional accounts and progress synchronization. In local testing, we verified the observation, photography, decision, and rover-return interactions for Surveyor 3 and Viking 1. Both expedition journals retained their separate decisions after reloading.

Super Intelligence disclosure

Google Gemini generated the fictional prologue film. Its still image comes from the same footage. Both carry a visible AI-generation watermark. The prologue narration uses ElevenLabs and a short macOS speech insert. The 30-second demo uses Kokoro-generated English narration over footage captured directly in the game. OpenAI Codex assisted with generating and revising portions of the code, testing, and drafting documentation and submission text.
